units.subject: Chemistry
units.title: Periodicity: Classification of Elements and the Periodic Law
objectives: Explain why elements are classified and describe the development from Mendeleev's table to the modern periodic table.
State the modern periodic law and relate groups and periods to recurring electronic structure and chemical properties.
units.body:
PERIODICITY — CLASSIFICATION OF ELEMENTS AND THE PERIODIC LAW

As the number of known elements increased, studying each element separately became difficult. Chemists therefore developed systems for classifying elements so that elements with similar properties could be grouped and their behaviour compared. The periodic table arranges elements by atomic number and displays recurring patterns in their physical and chemical properties.

MENDELEEV’S PERIODIC TABLE
Dmitri Mendeleev arranged elements largely in order of increasing atomic weight while placing elements with similar chemical properties in the same groups. He left gaps where he believed undiscovered elements belonged and predicted properties of some of them. The later discovery of elements such as gallium and germanium supported the usefulness of his predictions. However, arranging strictly by atomic weight produced anomalies, so some elements were placed out of strict mass order to preserve chemical similarities.

MODERN PERIODIC LAW
Henry Moseley’s work showed that atomic number, rather than atomic weight, is the more fundamental basis for arranging elements. The modern periodic law states that the physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers. When elements are arranged in increasing atomic number, similar outer-electron arrangements recur at regular intervals and related chemical properties appear in groups.

PERIODS, GROUPS AND ELECTRONIC STRUCTURE
Horizontal rows are periods; vertical columns are groups. Elements in the same group commonly have similar valence-electron arrangements and therefore show related chemical behaviour. Across a period, properties change progressively as nuclear charge and electron arrangement change. Down a group, additional electron shells affect atomic size and other properties. The source compares alkali metals, alkaline-earth metals and halogens: alkali metals have one outer electron and commonly form +1 ions; alkaline-earth metals have two outer electrons and commonly form +2 ions; halogens have seven outer electrons and commonly form -1 ions. Reactivity trends differ between groups, so comparisons must specify the family and trend being discussed.

WHY PERIODIC CLASSIFICATION IS USEFUL
The periodic table helps predict valency, likely ion formation, similarities between elements, and broad physical and chemical behaviour. It provides a systematic reference for studying elements and their compounds. When answering examination questions, distinguish Mendeleev’s periodic law (properties related to atomic weights) from the modern periodic law (properties related to atomic numbers), and explain the role of groups, periods and outer-shell electrons rather than merely memorising definitions.

SOURCE BOUNDARY
This is a lesson draft mapped to the First-Term SS2 Chemistry source’s opening Periodicity section. It does not replace the remaining First-Term topics on periodic trends, redox, ionic theory, electrolysis and electrochemical cells, nor the Second- and Third-Term schemes. The source contains worked examples and diagrams that still require page-level visual review.

units.subject: Chemistry
units.title: Periodic Trends in Physical Properties
objectives: Explain periodic trends in atomic and ionic radii, ionization energy, electron affinity, electronegativity and metallic character.
Use nuclear charge, shielding, electron configuration and atomic size to explain comparisons and exceptions.
units.body:
PERIODIC TRENDS IN PHYSICAL PROPERTIES

Many properties of elements depend on electronic configuration and vary periodically with atomic number. Important periodic properties include atomic and ionic radii, ionization energy, electron affinity, electronegativity and metallic character. These trends help explain and predict how atoms form ions and react.

ATOMIC RADIUS
Atomic radius is an estimate of atomic size. Because the electron cloud has no sharp boundary, different measures are used. Covalent radius is approximately half the distance between the nuclei of two identical atoms joined by a single covalent bond. Van der Waals radius is half the distance between neighbouring non-bonded atoms of the same element in adjacent molecules; it is generally larger than covalent radius. Metallic radius is half the internuclear distance between neighbouring atoms in a metallic lattice.

Across a period, atomic radius generally decreases from left to right because nuclear charge increases while added electrons enter the same principal shell. The stronger effective attraction draws the electron cloud closer to the nucleus. Down a group, atomic radius generally increases because additional occupied shells place the outer electrons farther from the nucleus and increase shielding.

IONIC RADIUS AND ISOELECTRONIC SPECIES
A cation forms when an atom loses electrons; its radius is generally smaller than that of the parent atom because the remaining electrons experience greater attraction and a shell may be removed. An anion forms when an atom gains electrons; its radius is generally larger than that of the parent atom because electron-electron repulsion increases while nuclear charge remains unchanged. Isoelectronic species have the same number of electrons. Within an isoelectronic series, radius decreases as nuclear charge increases because the same electron population is attracted more strongly.

IONIZATION ENERGY
Ionization energy is the energy required to remove an electron from an isolated gaseous atom in its ground state. Successive ionization energies increase because each electron removed leaves a more positively charged ion that holds its remaining electrons more strongly. A particularly large jump occurs when removal begins to disturb a stable inner-shell configuration after the valence electrons have been removed. Ionization energy is affected by atomic size, nuclear charge, shielding, orbital penetration and electronic configuration. It generally increases across a period and decreases down a group, although subshell stability and electron pairing cause exceptions.

ELECTRON AFFINITY, ELECTRONEGATIVITY AND METALLIC CHARACTER
Electron affinity concerns the energy change when a gaseous atom gains an electron. Electronegativity is the relative tendency of an atom in a chemical bond to attract the shared electrons. They are related but not identical. Metallic character describes the tendency to lose electrons and form positive ions; it generally increases down a group and decreases across a period. Halogens tend to gain electrons readily, while noble gases have stable outer-shell configurations and low tendency to react. Trends should be explained using effective nuclear attraction, shielding, atomic size and electron configuration rather than treated as exception-free rules.

EXAM RESPONSE METHOD
When comparing sizes, first determine whether the species are atoms, ions or isoelectronic. For isoelectronic ions, compare nuclear charge. When explaining ionization-energy trends, identify the direction of the trend and state the relevant factors. Distinguish electron affinity (energy change on electron gain) from electronegativity (attraction for shared bonding electrons).

SOURCE BOUNDARY
This draft maps to First-Term Week 2, Periodic Trends in Physical Properties. It does not replace the original worked examples, numerical data, tables or diagrams. Those visual and calculation elements require page-level review before delivery.

practice.question: Out of metallic radius and covalent radius of an element, which is larger and why?
practice.answer_locator: Authored model answer aligned to the source explanation of metallic and covalent radii.
practice.answer: The metallic radius is generally larger. Metallic radius is measured as half the distance between neighbouring atoms in a metallic lattice, whereas covalent radius is half the distance between nuclei of atoms joined by a covalent bond. Covalent bonds hold the bonded atoms closer together.
practice.explanation: Identify the larger radius and explain the difference in interatomic distance and bonding.

marking.criterion: Explains that covalently bonded atoms are closer together.

units.subject: Chemistry
units.title: Concept of Oxidation and Reduction
objectives: Explain oxidation and reduction using classical, electron-transfer and oxidation-number concepts.
Apply oxidation-number rules to identify oxidation, reduction, oxidising agents and reducing agents in reactions.
units.body:
OXIDATION AND REDUCTION — REDOX CONCEPTS AND OXIDATION NUMBERS

Oxidation and reduction occur together in redox reactions. Everyday examples include rusting and combustion; industrial examples include electroplating and metal extraction. The source introduces the classical definitions, electron-transfer definitions and oxidation-number approach.

CLASSICAL AND ELECTRON-TRANSFER DEFINITIONS
In the classical concept, oxidation involves addition of oxygen or an electronegative radical, or removal of hydrogen or an electropositive radical. Reduction involves addition of hydrogen or an electropositive radical, or removal of oxygen or an electronegative radical. In the electron-transfer concept, oxidation is loss of one or more electrons, while reduction is gain of one or more electrons. These occur simultaneously because electrons lost by one reacting species are gained by another. The reducing agent donates electrons and is itself oxidised; the oxidising agent accepts electrons and is itself reduced.

OXIDATION NUMBER
Oxidation number (oxidation state) is a formal value assigned to an atom using agreed rules for allocating bonding electrons. It is useful where electron transfer is not represented as a simple transfer of whole electrons. In a free element, the oxidation number is zero. For a monatomic ion, it equals the ion charge. Fluorine is -1 in its compounds. Hydrogen is usually +1, except in metal hydrides where it is -1. Oxygen is usually -2, but is -1 in peroxides and has positive values in compounds with fluorine. The sum of oxidation numbers in a neutral compound is zero; in a polyatomic ion, the sum equals the ion charge. Group 1 metals are usually +1 and Group 2 metals usually +2 in compounds.

A rise in oxidation number indicates oxidation; a fall indicates reduction. The oxidising agent undergoes a decrease in oxidation number, while the reducing agent undergoes an increase. A redox reaction can be separated into oxidation and reduction half-reactions: the oxidation half-reaction shows electron loss and the reduction half-reaction shows electron gain. The number of electrons lost and gained must balance when the half-reactions are combined.

HOW TO ANSWER REDOX QUESTIONS
First assign oxidation numbers using the rules, then compare the relevant atoms before and after reaction. An increase identifies oxidation; a decrease identifies reduction. Identify the oxidising agent as the species reduced and the reducing agent as the species oxidised. When a question asks which substance is oxidised or reduced, state the substance and briefly support the answer with the oxidation-number change or oxygen/hydrogen transfer.

SOURCE BOUNDARY
This lesson draft maps to First-Term Week 3, Concept of Oxidation and Reduction. It does not cover Week 4 redox balancing or later electrochemistry. The original source contains equations and worked examples whose exact formatting and balancing still require page-level checking.

practice.question: Define the terms oxidation and reduction.
practice.answer_locator: Authored model answer aligned to the source's classical and electron-transfer definitions.
practice.answer: Oxidation is loss of one or more electrons or an increase in oxidation number; in the classical concept it can also mean addition of oxygen or removal of hydrogen. Reduction is gain of one or more electrons or a decrease in oxidation number; classically it can mean removal of oxygen or addition of hydrogen.
practice.explanation: Accept a consistent definition using the electron-transfer or oxidation-number concept; classical definitions may also be stated.

practice.question_locator: First-Term source, Week 3 EVALUATION, question 5: Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2.
practice.question: In the reaction Fe2O3(s) + 3CO(g) → 2Fe(s) + 3CO2(g), identify the substance reduced and the substance oxidised.
practice.answer_locator: Authored model answer using oxidation-number changes.
practice.answer: Iron(III) oxide (Fe2O3) is reduced to iron (Fe) because iron changes from oxidation number +3 to 0. Carbon monoxide (CO) is oxidised to carbon dioxide (CO2) because carbon changes from +2 to +4.
practice.explanation: Reduction is a decrease in oxidation number; oxidation is an increase. Identify the reactants undergoing each change.

marking.criterion: Identifies Fe2O3 as the substance reduced.
Identifies CO as the substance oxidised.
